messages.subject: Re: Export Survey Coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Helena, list:

1. The coordinates of all samples in a survey that has been created from
a Distance design are listed on the 3rd page of the Results tab of the
survey details (Sampler location list).  This isn't a great format for
importing into other packages such as GIS however.

2. The survey has an associated sample layer, which you can see in the
Data tab of the project browser.  This has an ESRI shapefile linked to
it, which holds the geographic information (the coordinates of each
sample).  The shapefile is located in the data folder associated with
the project, and you can find it's name by looking in the Geographic tab
of the data layer properties for that sample layer.  (Click on the
sample layer name in the tree view on the left hand side of the data
browser, right click, choose data layer properties).  You can take this
shapefile and import it into almost every other GIS.

3. If you don't have access to a commercial GIS, but you want to work
with the shapefile, you might consider accessing it using the free
software R.  I don't know anything about this, but at our workshops last
summer, one of the participants Ben Best gave a very nice talk on this
and other free GIS tools.  He pointed out the sp and rgdal libraries for
R, and the R spatial task view, which has up to date info about
manipulating spatial data in R, at
http://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Views/Spatial.html

4. I hope to significantly improve the ability for Distance to import
and export GIS data in the next release.

Hope this helps,

  - len

messages.body_plain:
Danielle/List:

If you are interested in making sophisticated plots of your detection
function (I define sophisticated to include the tiling approach you
describe), I would not employ the cut-and-paste graphics approach, but
rather I would move to another piece of software.  Export the data (not
the graphic) of your detection function to another package (See
"Exporting CDS results from analysis details results" in Chapter 8 of
the users guide).

You can then send the data to Excel (see macro on the support page of
the Distance website), or recreate the graphic in R (using a script also
found in Chapter 8 of the users guide).  Using Excel or R, you have
utter and complete control of every aspect of the graph (not just the
fonts, but line widths,  etc. etc.)

Let me know if you need more of a boost than that.

messages.subject: Re: temporal relpicates etc
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marcel, (list,)

Here are my thoughts.

Your design means you can only make valid design-based inferences about
density in the local area covered by your 10 transects.  For making
inferences about density in the wider area (i.e., the entire forest
where you randomly placed the whole system of transects), you
effectively have 1 replicate.  This caveat needs to be clear when you
report your results.

10 is rather a small number of transects for getting good estimates of
local spatial variance -- would have been better if you could have
gotten 20 or so -- but I appreciate these things aren't easy!

Regarding walking some transects 3 times and some 5.  This is not a big
problem.  In the analysis, pool all visits to the transects together and
multiply the transect length by the number of visits.  So, if you
visited transect A 3 times, and it was 1km long, the line length in
Distance will be 3km.  For transect B, also 1km long but visited 5 times
the line length is 5km.  The only potential minor problem is that you
loose the pooling robustness property of distance sampling estimators of
detection functions when coverage is not uniform through the area of
interest (see the Intro to distance sampling book if some of these terms
don't mean anything to you).  However, if we can consider that the
transect visits missed were "at random" -- ie not deliberately chosen to
miss the furthest transects, or those in the densest forest, etc, then
there is no problem in this case.

I noted that one thing that prevented you from surveying 5 times was
earthquakes.  Your life certainly seems more exiting than mine!

I also noted that you wanted to pool within time slots -- I'm not sure
why one would want to do this - why not simply pool all the data on each
transect?  Presumably true density does not change between time slots;
if you are worried about detection function changing over time slots,
consider (1) that so long as it does not change too much then pooling
robustness means you don't have to worry about it; (2) if it does change
a lot then for the species where you have lots of detections you could
try using MCDS to look at it.

Regarding cluster sizes, I think you have no alternative but to use just
the visual detections for cluster size, since you likely have no
estimate of cluster size at all for the acoustic encounters.  In the
case where one has good estimates for visual and poor ones for acoustic,
a size bias regression approach may work if there are no acoustic
detections close to the line.  In your case, you might want to use the
mean cluster size for visual only detections, or you could consider
doing a size bias regression for visual detections -- but that would be
complicated, and if you have good group size estimates from visual it
seems un-necessary.  Either way, you can enter the population mean group
size estimate you obtain into subsequent calculations using a multiplier.

I do worry a bit if you have visual and acoustic detections together
that in combining them you will end up with a nasty spiked detection
function (e.g., Intro to distance sampling figure 2.1), which is hard to
model reliably, particularly with relatively small sample sizes.  It
depends on what proportion of groups are detectable acoustically.  If it
is high at small distances, but you also see them, and then drops off
slowly with increasing distance, then the combined detection function
may be shallow.  However, if only a small fraction of troupes vocalize
while you are surveying, but these vocalizations are detectable at large
distances, then you will have a steep visual detection function combined
with a shallow acoustic detection function where the latter peaks at a
detection probability at zero distance of less than one, and combined
this leads to something like fig 2.1.  I don't know which of these you have.

For the two species with few observations, I think you should be very
cautious about doing anything with them, particularly if the combined
detection function is spiked.  If, on the other hand, you know it is
shallow, you might be able to make some preliminary inferences by
fitting only 1 or 2 parameter detection function models.  But I would be
very cautious about this -- perhaps better to wait until more data have
been collected.

To repeat what I said at the top, I view your biggest problem as the
survey design, if you want to make inferences about numbers in the whole
forest, rather than just the local area.

Hope this helps,

  - Len Thomas

a size bias regression approach may work if there are no acoustic
detections close to the line.  In your case, you might want to use the
mean cluster size for visual only detections, or you could consider
doing a size bias regression for visual detections -- but that would be
complicated, and if you have good group size estimates from visual it
seems un-necessary.  Either way, you can enter the population mean group
size estimate you obtain into subsequent calculations using a multiplier.

I do worry a bit if you have visual and acoustic detections together
that in combining them you will end up with a nasty spiked detection
function (e.g., Intro to distance sampling figure 2.1), which is hard to
model reliably, particularly with relatively small sample sizes.  It
depends on what proportion of groups are detectable acoustically.  If it
is high at small distances, but you also see them, and then drops off
slowly with increasing distance, then the combined detection function
may be shallow.  However, if only a small fraction of troupes vocalize
while you are surveying, but these vocalizations are detectable at large
distances, then you will have a steep visual detection function combined
with a shallow acoustic detection function where the latter peaks at a
detection probability at zero distance of less than one, and combined
this leads to something like fig 2.1.  I don't know which of these you have.

For the two species with few observations, I think you should be very
cautious about doing anything with them, particularly if the combined
detection function is spiked.  If, on the other hand, you know it is
shallow, you might be able to make some preliminary inferences by
fitting only 1 or 2 parameter detection function models.  But I would be
very cautious about this -- perhaps better to wait until more data have
been collected.

To repeat what I said at the top, I view your biggest problem as the
survey design, if you want to make inferences about numbers in the whole
forest, rather than just the local area.

Hope this helps,

  - Len Thomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi list,
we are planning a line survey to estimate roe deer densities in 9 different forest patches.
The main aim of the study is to compare densities of deer among areas (and later on to compare estimates over time).
Since we have to conduct the study at night and by vehicle, the survey design needs to be restricted to forest roads.
In 4 areas, it is possible to distribute 15-20 transects systematically over each forest.
However, in the other 5 areas, the terrain is rather hilly and hence the roads are not distributed systematically but rather follow contour lines. Actually, the roads form "roundtrips". Within each area, the tracks are quite evenly distributed but it is not possible to identify single roads which could be used as a proxy for a transect.
Would it be ok to treat every new km of a roundtrip as a "new" transect or how (if at all) can one split the whole road network in suitable transects?

I know that the entire road-design approach bears serious design-based inference problems but maybe someone has a good idea to make the best out off a difficult setting?

Kind regards,

Christian

yields abundance, then I assume all data should be corrected in the same=20=

way for further analyses (AIC, CCA) relating abundance to habitat=20

=20

Hi James,

> >Now, I wish to adjust my counts (number of detections within 100-m=20

radius) to account for variation in detection probability resulting from=20=

variation in shrub cover.

The easy way, assuming each point is entered as a sample in Distance, is=20=

to set up a new Model Definition and tick the box to estimate density by=20=

sample in the Estimate tab.  If you want abundance by point, it's simply=20=

density*pi*w^2 where w is truncation distance.

However, if you want to calculate abundance in each sample (point) by=20
hand, you can use the Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator:    estimated=20

abundance =3D sum(1/estimated p_i) where the sum is over all animals coun=
ted=20
at the point, and p_i is the estimated probability of detecting the ith=20=

animal, given it is within the truncation distance.  To calculate p_i, se=
e=20
the Distance online help -- look in the index under Detection function,=20=

formulae, about.  Note that if you don't have animal level covariates=20

(which it appears you don't) then p_i will be the same for all animals at=
=20
a point, so the above reduces to    estimated abundance =3D n/p where n i=
s=20
the count at the point and p is the estimated probability of detecting an=

=20
animal given it is within the truncation distance.

As an aside, assuming that your stands vary in size, then by locating one=
=20
point in each stand you have a design with a different proportion of the=20=

stand area surveyed in each point (different "coverage probability" in=20=

each stand).  If you're also interested in calculating an average density=

=20
over all stands, you'll need to take this into account.  You could=20

calculate a weighted mean of the stand densities, with the weight being=20=

the proportion of the stand area surveyed.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

Hi James,

I don't think you need to do anything by hand, unless you're a=20

masochist!    I wasn't 100% clear in my previous message so I'll try to=20=

lay it out better here.  For that reason I'm also cc'ing this to the list=

,=20
in case anyone else wants to do the same thing.

I think you want to fit the detection function using all your data, but=20=

with habitat as a covariate (which you have done), but then *predict* the=

=20
probability of detection at each point, given the habitat type of the=20

point and that the animal is present within the truncation distance.  You=
=20
then want to calculate density (or abundance) at each point using this=20=

habitat-specific probability of detection.

You can do this in the multiple covariate engine of Distance in the Model=
=20
Definition | Estimate tab.  Under "Quantities to estimate and level of=20=

resolution", for the Density and the detection function rows, tick both=20=

the "Global" and "Sample" columns.  Make sure you have habitat as a=20

covariate.  For more about this, see the online help, Chapter 9, Defining=

=20
MCDS models, Estimating the detection function at multiple levels.

The output you will get will be density for each point, and p_i for=20

animals at each point too.  (You will also get abundance for each point,=20=

but there's a bug in Distance where the area used to calculate this is=20=

currently wrong so it's acutally abundance for the whole study area=20

assuming density at that point applies to the whole study area -- this bu=

g=20
is fixed in the next version of Distance to be released.)

You *can* calculate probability of detection by hand if you really want=20=

to =96 but it's going to require some work.  We want p_i, the probability=
 of=20
detecting an animal at each point, given that it is within the truncation=
=20
distance.  Note, this isn't the probability of detecting the animal at=20=

it's observed distance -- it's the probability given that the animal was=20=

somewhere between 0 and w.  We could use the observed distances but then=20=

estimation tends to be less reliable -- for more on this see the MCDS=20

chapter of the up-coming Advanced Distance Sampling book.  Because we're=20=

integrating out the distance component, the only covariate left is=20

habitat, so that means the p_i's will be the same for all animals at each=
=20
point, given the amount of shrub cover.  So what you need to do is progra=
m=20
Excel (or something better) to work out probability of detection for a=20=

given covariate level and distance, and then program Excel (or whatever)=20=

to integrate this function between 0 and w, using numerical integration=20=

such as Simpson's rule.  As you can see, it's probably easier to let=20
Distance do it!

Specific replies to your questions about estimating p below, should you=20=

still
want to do it.

Cheers,

Hi Nick, list,

What you're proposing is what we sometimes call "spatial modeling"=20

or "spatial density surface estimation".  I'll attempt an answer, but I'm=
=20
no expert so others may want to contribute more.  Also, there's some stuf=

f=20
on this in Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book.

To begin with, you need to do the detection function modeling in=20

Distance.  You could either stratify by habitat, or put habitat in as a=20=

factor covariate in the MCDS engine.  If you have enough data, and no=20

problems such as avoidance, rounding, etc, then you could try both and le=
t=20
AIC tell you which is better.  If using MCDS then you could include other=
=20
covariates too.  Once you've finished this modeling, you want an estimate=

=20
of detection probability by point (p_k) (Note, I'm omitting hats from=20

estimates to avoid cumbersome text notation.  Also, for now, I'm assuming=
=20
you don't have any species level covariates such as cluster size).  To do=
=20
this, you ask for density by sample, as in my reply to  "Adjusting counts=

=20
for delectability and covariates" (Tucker, 11 May 2004).

Now you need to incorporate the estimates of p_k into the spatial model=20=

for the bird counts.  To my knowledge there are three ways to do this:

1. Divide the observed count at each point n_k by the estimated p_k to ge=

t=20
an estimate of abundance at each point N_k.  This abundance is non-
integer, so:

2. you might want to divide N_k by the area of each point (pi*w^2) to get=

=20
an estimated density at each point D_k.  Doesn't make much difference=20

really.  Either way, your GLM or GAM will no longer have a Poisson error=20=

term as the response variable is non-integer -- perhaps a Gamma?=20

3. Retain the n_k as the response variable in a Poisson model, but use=20=

pi*nu_k^2 as an offset, where nu_k is the effective detection radius for=20=

that point.

Personally, I prefer 3 as you get to keep the discrete nature of the=20
counts.  However method 3 doesn't work if you have any species level=20

covariates, such as sex of bird or cluster size.  In that case, you don't=
=20
know what the effective detection radius is when you observe no birds --=20=

but you do know that the estimate of density is 0.  If you have species=20=

level covariates in 1 or 2 you estimate N_k by the sum of 1/p_i for each=20=

bird i detected at the point.  There is a section of the online manual=20=

that says how to calculate p_i for each animal given the parameter=20
estimates of the detection function.

In practice, two problems usually present themselves:

1. Overdispersion.  Often many points have 0 birds seen, so you get data=20=

with lots of zeros and relatively few high counts (or high D_ks if the=20=

p_ks are sometimes small).  Can be hard to model.  Can perhaps investigat=

e=20
the various zero-inflated models that are out there?

2. Variance estimation.  How does one incorporate the variance due to=20

estimating the detection function in the final variance estimate from the=
=20
spatial model?  An easy way is a nonparametric bootstrap or jackknife of=20=

points, but you need plenty of points for this.  Various parametric=20
bootstraps have been proposed - I think there is something on this in=20

Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book.  It may be possible to=20=

do something analytic based on the delta method -- don't know.

So, hope this helps -- as I said others may be able to contribute more.=20=

I'll answer your second question in a separate email.

Cheers,

 - Len

intelligent use of the program.  Also, I've found in general that people=20=

who have a poor understanding of the program options also have a poor=20

understanding of how to design surveys and implement field methods that=20=

give reliable results. Just my prejudice I guess.

> >already have a figure for density on the print-out and they are happy!
> >My question: What combination of criteria would lead you to reject a
> >density estimate outright?

I'm afraid it's not that simple.  Getting a reliable estimate requires=20=

more than just an "adequate" sample size of observations, and the require=
d=20
sample size depends on factors such as the type of survey (points require=

=20
more than lines), and shape of the detection function (wide shoulders=20

require fewer observations to accurately model).  Also, remember that you=

=20
also need a "decent" sample size of lines or points for reliable=20
estimation of the encounter rate variance.

Here's a very rough checklist for initial assessment of a study:

- were the lines/points laid out according to a randomized survey design?=
=20=20
Ideally there should be 20 or more lines or points - many fewer than that=
=20
and I'd doubt the encounter rate variance estimates.  If the analysis is=20=

stratified, you'd like 20 lines per stratum if possible.

- is g(0) likely to be 1?

- is animal movement likely to be a problem? (is there evasive movement,=20=

or do animals move at more than 1/3-half the speed of the observer for=20=

line transects; were the point transects performed over a "long" time=20
period (ie not a snapshot)

- were distances measured accurately?

- does the detection function have a wide shoulder?

- is the sample size of observations reasonable? (60-80 recommended,=20
although for wide shoulders and line transects can get away with far=20

fewer). If the detection function is estimated by stratum, you'd like 60-=

80 observations by stratum if possible.

- does the analysis look like it was performed competently?

- do the reported results give both the estimate and CI/CV, and=20
interpretation of the results take account of the uncertainty in the=20
estimate.

I've probably forgotten something, but hope this helps.  Perhaps someone=20=

else will be willing to stick their neck out and offer more absolute rule=

s=20
of thumb!

 - Len

Hi James,

> >Now, I wish to adjust my counts (number of detections within 100-m=20
radius) to account for variation in detection probability resulting from=20=

variation in shrub cover.

The easy way, assuming each point is entered as a sample in Distance, is=20=

to set up a new Model Definition and tick the box to estimate density by=20=

sample in the Estimate tab.  If you want abundance by point, it's simply=20=

density*pi*w^2 where w is truncation distance.

However, if you want to calculate abundance in each sample (point) by=20
hand, you can use the Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator:    estimated=20
abundance =3D sum(1/estimated p_i) where the sum is over all animals coun=
ted=20
at the point, and p_i is the estimated probability of detecting the ith=20=

animal, given it is within the truncation distance.  To calculate p_i, se=
e=20
the Distance online help -- look in the index under Detection function,=20=

formulae, about.  Note that if you don't have animal level covariates=20
(which it appears you don't) then p_i will be the same for all animals at=
=20
a point, so the above reduces to    estimated abundance =3D n/p where n i=
s=20
the count at the point and p is the estimated probability of detecting an=
=20
animal given it is within the truncation distance.

As an aside, assuming that your stands vary in size, then by locating one=
=20
point in each stand you have a design with a different proportion of the=20=

stand area surveyed in each point (different "coverage probability" in=20=

each stand).  If you're also interested in calculating an average density=
=20
over all stands, you'll need to take this into account.  You could=20
calculate a weighted mean of the stand densities, with the weight being=20=

the proportion of the stand area surveyed.

Hope this helps,

I think you want to fit the detection function using all your data, but=20=

with habitat as a covariate (which you have done), but then *predict* the=

probability of detection at each point, given the habitat type of the=20
point and that the animal is present within the truncation distance.  You=
=20
then want to calculate density (or abundance) at each point using this=20=

habitat-specific probability of detection.

You can do this in the multiple covariate engine of Distance in the Model=
=20

distance.  Note, this isn't the probability of detecting the animal at=20=

m=20

Hi Nick, list,

What you're proposing is what we sometimes call "spatial modeling"=20
or "spatial density surface estimation".  I'll attempt an answer, but I'm=
=20
no expert so others may want to contribute more.  Also, there's some stuf=
f=20
on this in Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book.

To begin with, you need to do the detection function modeling in=20
Distance.  You could either stratify by habitat, or put habitat in as a=20=

factor covariate in the MCDS engine.  If you have enough data, and no=20
problems such as avoidance, rounding, etc, then you could try both and le=
t=20
AIC tell you which is better.  If using MCDS then you could include other=
=20
covariates too.  Once you've finished this modeling, you want an estimate=
=20
of detection probability by point (p_k) (Note, I'm omitting hats from=20
estimates to avoid cumbersome text notation.  Also, for now, I'm assuming=
=20
you don't have any species level covariates such as cluster size).  To do=
=20
this, you ask for density by sample, as in my reply to  "Adjusting counts=
=20
for delectability and covariates" (Tucker, 11 May 2004).

Now you need to incorporate the estimates of p_k into the spatial model=20=

for the bird counts.  To my knowledge there are three ways to do this:

1. Divide the observed count at each point n_k by the estimated p_k to ge=
t=20
an estimate of abundance at each point N_k.  This abundance is non-
integer, so:

2. you might want to divide N_k by the area of each point (pi*w^2) to get=
=20
an estimated density at each point D_k.  Doesn't make much difference=20
really.  Either way, your GLM or GAM will no longer have a Poisson error=20=

term as the response variable is non-integer -- perhaps a Gamma?=20

3. Retain the n_k as the response variable in a Poisson model, but use=20=

pi*nu_k^2 as an offset, where nu_k is the effective detection radius for=20=

that point.

Personally, I prefer 3 as you get to keep the discrete nature of the=20
counts.  However method 3 doesn't work if you have any species level=20
covariates, such as sex of bird or cluster size.  In that case, you don't=
=20
know what the effective detection radius is when you observe no birds --=20=

but you do know that the estimate of density is 0.  If you have species=20=

level covariates in 1 or 2 you estimate N_k by the sum of 1/p_i for each=20=

bird i detected at the point.  There is a section of the online manual=20=

that says how to calculate p_i for each animal given the parameter=20
estimates of the detection function.

In practice, two problems usually present themselves:

1. Overdispersion.  Often many points have 0 birds seen, so you get data=20=

with lots of zeros and relatively few high counts (or high D_ks if the=20=

p_ks are sometimes small).  Can be hard to model.  Can perhaps investigat=
e=20
the various zero-inflated models that are out there?

2. Variance estimation.  How does one incorporate the variance due to=20
estimating the detection function in the final variance estimate from the=
=20
spatial model?  An easy way is a nonparametric bootstrap or jackknife of=20=

points, but you need plenty of points for this.  Various parametric=20
bootstraps have been proposed - I think there is something on this in=20
Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book.  It may be possible to=20=

do something analytic based on the delta method -- don't know.

So, hope this helps -- as I said others may be able to contribute more.=20=

I'll answer your second question in a separate email.

Cheers,

 - Len

Argh!  Hopefully you can do your bit in training people to make=20
intelligent use of the program.  Also, I've found in general that people=20=

who have a poor understanding of the program options also have a poor=20
understanding of how to design surveys and implement field methods that=20=

give reliable results. Just my prejudice I guess.

> >Very small sample sizes often lead to very high variation in estimated
> >density but this is regularly justified by saying that "the 'real' value=

> >must be within the confidence intervals somewhere". What is the simple
> >answer to this question? I can tell people that a sample size of 10 will=

> >give you little information on density, or that a CV of over 20%
> >suggests a pretty inaccurate estimate, but by that point most people
> >already have a figure for density on the print-out and they are happy!
> >My question: What combination of criteria would lead you to reject a
> >density estimate outright?

I'm afraid it's not that simple.  Getting a reliable estimate requires=20=

more than just an "adequate" sample size of observations, and the require=
d=20
sample size depends on factors such as the type of survey (points require=
=20
more than lines), and shape of the detection function (wide shoulders=20
require fewer observations to accurately model).  Also, remember that you=
=20
also need a "decent" sample size of lines or points for reliable=20
estimation of the encounter rate variance.

Here's a very rough checklist for initial assessment of a study:

- were the lines/points laid out according to a randomized survey design?=
=20=20
Ideally there should be 20 or more lines or points - many fewer than that=
=20
and I'd doubt the encounter rate variance estimates.  If the analysis is=20=

stratified, you'd like 20 lines per stratum if possible.

- is g(0) likely to be 1?

- is animal movement likely to be a problem? (is there evasive movement,=20=

or do animals move at more than 1/3-half the speed of the observer for=20=

line transects; were the point transects performed over a "long" time=20
period (ie not a snapshot)

- were distances measured accurately?

- does the detection function have a wide shoulder?

- is the sample size of observations reasonable? (60-80 recommended,=20
although for wide shoulders and line transects can get away with far=20
fewer). If the detection function is estimated by stratum, you'd like 60-=

80 observations by stratum if possible.

- does the analysis look like it was performed competently?

- do the reported results give both the estimate and CI/CV, and=20
interpretation of the results take account of the uncertainty in the=20
estimate.

I've probably forgotten something, but hope this helps.  Perhaps someone=20=

else will be willing to stick their neck out and offer more absolute rule=
s=20
of thumb!

 - Len

Matt, a few brief thoughts.  Overall, your strategy seems fine.  A=20
different strategy that you might consider is to use a measure of=20
urbanization as a covariate, and use multiple covariate distance sampling=
,=20
which is in current versions of Distance.  This reduces the problems due=20=

to small sample sizes.

detections in the first interval, especially in the most urbanized=20
stratum.  I wonder if this might be related to the impossibility of=20
locating points at random in an urban environment?  Perhaps habitat close=
=20

environment, might your jays tend to approach the observer, so be recorde=
d=20

that you get a good model fit.  I suspect default model selection in=20

e=20
data.  I would be inclined to stick with say the half-normal model with n=
o=20
adjustment terms, to try to get a more robust analysis.  (I would however=
=20
include a measure of urbanization as a covariate in the half-normal=20
detection fn.)

> > But DISTANCE reports the est(N) = 105.00

I believe for abundance (whole animals) it rounds to the nearest animal.
> > Further, DISTANCE reports the est(density) = 0.0053775 which agrees with

> > my hand calculation, but does nor agree with the abundance estimate from

> > DISTANCE.
> >
> > I am going to be calculating abundance estimates by hand for my final

> > need to pool surveys over the all temporal strata to fit the detection

> > thus came up with an incorrect abundance estimate.  I can't figure out how

> > to make it use the correct totals for line length within the temporal

> > strata.
> >
Post-stratification is for separating out types of objects (eg
species).  If you use a strata definition based on time then you can
compute estimates by strata to do what you want.  However, if you have
both time and area strata then you are out of luck with either CDS or
MCDS.  You can however handle both time and area with the MRDS.  You
would fit a single detection function and then run density estimates by
strata for each time using the fitted global detection function.
However, that won't get you covariances between temporal density
estimates due to using a common detection function.  I'd need to think
about that one some more.  Probably just needs some more programming.

> > Values were: n=181, expected cluster size = 1.7008), f(0) = 0.0063315, A =
> > 194375000, L=1812262.
> > Thus est(N)should be (181*.0063315*1.7008*194375000)/(2*1812262) = 104.5268
> > But DISTANCE reports the est(N) = 105.00
> >
> >
I believe for abundance (whole animals) it rounds to the nearest animal.
> > Further, DISTANCE reports the est(density) = 0.0053775 which agrees with

> > my hand calculation, but does nor agree with the abundance estimate from

> > DISTANCE.
> >
> > I am going to be calculating abundance estimates by hand for my final

> > analysis, because I have temporal strata (seasons within years), but I

> > need to pool surveys over the all temporal strata to fit the detection

> > functions, due to sample size restrictions.
> >
> > That brings up a second question - can I use post-stratification to get

> > DISTANCE to calculate the abundance estimates within temporal strata,

> > while pooling all of the data across seasons to fit the detection

> > functions?  I tried using post-stratification by temporal strata (season-

> > year), but DISTANCE wasn't using the line lengths for the temporal

> > strata.  Instaed, within each strata, it used the entire line length and

> > thus came up with an incorrect abundance estimate.  I can't figure out how
> > to make it use the correct totals for line length within the temporal
> > strata.
> >
Post-stratification is for separating out types of objects (eg
species).  If you use a strata definition based on time then you can
compute estimates by strata to do what you want.  However, if you have
both time and area strata then you are out of luck with either CDS or
MCDS.  You can however handle both time and area with the MRDS.  You
would fit a single detection function and then run density estimates by
strata for each time using the fitted global detection function.
However, that won't get you covariances between temporal density
estimates due to using a common detection function.  I'd need to think
about that one some more.  Probably just needs some more programming.
